OppFi disclosed the California proceedings in its SEC filings as a material contingency, flagging the potential for an adverse determination to require suspension of new originations in the state. California accounted for a meaningful share of OppFi's total loan volume; the loss of access would have ranked among the largest single-state contractions in its operating history. By mid-2025, the California proceedings remained at the contested stage, with OppFi maintaining lending operations under the bank-partnership structure while litigation advanced. The DFPI had not obtained a final injunction or entered a final order as of the frozen snapshot date, though the administrative calendar was moving forward.

## Colorado: The Statutory True-Lender Path

Colorado took a different approach, codifying the true-lender standard in statute rather than relying on regulators to extrapolate it from existing law. [Senate Bill 21-093](https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/sb21-093), signed into law in 2021, created a statutory true-lender test under Colorado law: if a non-bank entity has the predominant economic interest in a loan — a defined standard incorporating risk retention, marketing, underwriting, and funding — that entity is the lender for purposes of Colorado's Uniform Consumer Credit Code rate restrictions.

Colorado's statutory codification was significant because it foreclosed the preemption argument at the definitional level. Unlike California, where OppFi could contest the DFPI's regulatory interpretation of existing law, Colorado's legislature had directly addressed and rejected the bank-export structure as applied to partnerships in which the fintech bore the predominant economic interest. The Colorado Attorney General pursued enforcement against rent-a-bank lenders following the bill's enactment, and OppFi disclosed Colorado among the jurisdictions where its ability to originate new loans faced ongoing legal challenge.

## Washington D.C. and the Eastern Seaboard Pressure

The District of Columbia enacted the True Lender Amendment Act, aligning D.C. lending law with the true-lender framework and enabling the D.C. Attorney General to pursue enforcement actions against fintech lenders operating under bank partnerships. OppFi disclosed D.C. proceedings in its public filings as part of its expanding multi-state litigation inventory.

New York presented structural rather than active enforcement pressure. New York's 25% civil usury cap for most consumer loans and its criminal usury provisions had long made the state effectively inaccessible to high-APR consumer lenders operating through any structure. The New York Department of Financial Services and the Office of the Attorney General had pursued enforcement against various rent-a-bank arrangements, and New York remained outside OppFi's addressable footprint throughout the 2021–2025 period. Minnesota and North Carolina emerged as active enforcement states by 2024, narrowing OppFi's accessible geography further.

## Addressable Market Compression

The cumulative effect of multi-state true-lender challenges was a progressive contraction in OppFi's available market. In its 2022, 2023, and 2024 annual filings, OppFi disclosed that it was not operating, had suspended operations, or faced material legal uncertainty in an expanding list of states, enumerating the jurisdictions as risk factors and flagging that adverse judicial or regulatory outcomes could require suspension of new originations pending appeal or statutory change.

| Jurisdiction | Status (as of frozen snapshot) | Legal Vehicle |
|---|---|---|
| Illinois | Suspended; litigation exhausted | PLPA statutory 36% cap; preemption challenge declined |
| California | Active but contested | CCFPL / DFPI administrative proceedings |
| Colorado | Restricted | SB 21-093 statutory true-lender test |
| Washington, D.C. | Restricted | True Lender Amendment Act; AG enforcement |
| New York | Not operating | Criminal usury; DFS/AG posture |
| Minnesota | Restricted | AG consumer-protection enforcement |
| North Carolina | Restricted | AG proceedings |

Each line in that table represented a population cohort of non-prime consumers that OppFi's underwriting algorithm could serve but its legal posture precluded. For a company whose total addressable market is defined by geography and APR tolerance, each adverse determination was simultaneously a legal loss and a revenue ceiling.

## Federal Crosscurrents: The CFPB's Arc

At the federal level, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau under Director Rohit Chopra was a consistent adversary of the bank-partnership model through 2024. The Bureau filed amicus briefs in state and federal litigation supporting true-lender arguments, used its supervisory authority to examine bank partners involved in fintech arrangements, and issued guidance signaling its view that non-bank platforms bearing predominant economic interest were the de facto lenders for consumer-protection purposes. OppFi's bank partners — FinWise, Capital Community, and First Electronic — all fell within the Bureau's examination reach as insured depositories, and the CFPB's scrutiny of program agreements added a federal dimension to what had primarily been a state-level fight.

The inauguration of the Trump administration in January 2025 altered the federal vector sharply. Chopra was dismissed, and the CFPB's leadership and posture shifted under acting directors aligned with the new administration's deregulatory philosophy. The Bureau's amicus practice in rent-a-bank cases softened materially, and active examination of bank-partnership structures decelerated. By mid-2025, CFPB enforcement activity against OppFi's category of lender had substantially diminished — though the structural hostility built into state statutes like Illinois's PLPA and Colorado's SB 21-093 remained unchanged regardless of federal posture. State law, once enacted, did not pivot with the federal political cycle.

## OppFi's Strategic Response and the Residual Wager

Against this backdrop, OppFi pursued a three-track legal strategy. The first track was litigation: challenging adverse state determinations in federal and state court, arguing Section 27 FDIA preemption and, where possible, procedural infirmities in the regulatory process. The second track was engagement: working with state legislators and regulators to negotiate operating parameters — rate schedules, disclosure requirements, or licensing arrangements — that could allow continued lending within a compliant framework. The third track was market prioritization: concentrating origination volume in lower-legal-risk jurisdictions, accepting compressed geography in exchange for operational clarity.

Schwartz addressed the litigation environment repeatedly on earnings calls, characterizing OppFi's bank partners as the genuine originating lenders under a documented and substantive program structure, disputing the regulatory characterizations of the partnership as a mere conduit. The company's legal disclosures throughout the 2022–2025 period consistently maintained that the bank-partnership model was lawful under applicable federal preemption doctrine while acknowledging the material risk that adverse outcomes could reduce operating markets and revenue.

The structural bet — that the bank-partnership model would survive state-level challenge in enough jurisdictions to sustain a viable national footprint — remained the central, unresolved wager of the OppFi investment thesis through the frozen snapshot. Each court docket and each state legislative session carried the potential to expand or contract the company's effective market by millions of eligible borrowers and tens of millions of dollars in potential originations. The litigation map was, inescapably, the business map.

chapters.title: Timeline from 2012 founding through SPAC listing and litigation milestones
chapters.body:
## From Kitchen Table to Capital Markets: The Founding Proposition

Schwartz launched Opportunity Financial in 2012 with a thesis that non-prime borrowers — salaried Americans with FICO scores below 650 — were underserved, not uncreditworthy. The bank-partnership model built around that thesis leveraged federal rate-exportation authority to serve borrowers nationally while avoiding state-by-state licensing constraints.

## The SPAC Pivot and the NYSE Listing

OppFi completed its combination with FG New America Acquisition Corp. in July 2021, listing on NYSE under the up-C structure common to founder-led fintech SPACs. The timing proved, in retrospect, almost precisely wrong — the listing arrived at a late-cycle moment just before the credit environment inflected adversely.

## True-Lender Litigation: The Long Reckoning

State attorneys general and regulators assembled true-lender challenges across California, Colorado, New York, and the District of Columbia — each adverse outcome compressing addressable market directly. (See *Litigation & Regulatory* chapter for detailed coverage.)

## The Credit-Cycle Trough: 2022–2023

Simultaneous with litigation, OppFi navigated the most difficult credit environment for non-prime lending in more than a decade. The 2022–2023 vintages experienced elevated charge-offs; SalaryTap was paused. (See *Earnings Story* and *Financial Deep Dive* for detailed coverage.)

## The 2024 Recovery

By fiscal 2024, tighter-underwritten cohorts were producing normalized charge-offs and sustainably positive profitability.

## Forward Catalysts

Three dynamics define OppFi's forward trajectory: (1) the litigation pipeline — binary events capable of adding or removing hundreds of millions of addressable origination volume; (2) multi-product expansion via the OppFi Card; and (3) the consumer-credit cycle. Whether the true-lender litigation crucible produces durable legal clarity or continued jurisdictional attrition remains the central unresolved question.

chapters.title: Litigation, credit cycle, funding, governance, regulatory, competitive risks
chapters.body:
## The True-Lender Crucible

The most existential risk OppFi carried into 2026 was true-lender litigation — the contested proposition that its bank partners, not OppFi, are the lenders entitled to federal rate preemption. Where that proposition fails, OppFi's product becomes unlawful. California, Colorado, Washington, D.C., and Illinois each pursued enforcement actions (see *Litigation & Regulatory* chapter for detailed coverage).

Each adverse outcome compressed OppFi's geographic addressable market in a compounding manner. As [OppFi 10-K filings on SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=OPFI&type=10-K) documented, the company was required to include growing state-by-state disclosure of jurisdictions where it had curtailed or ceased originating loans. By late 2024, the map of inactive or legally contested geographies included several of the most populous US states. Management characterised the situation as a litigation portfolio rather than a regulatory posture — each case individuated, each appealable — but the cumulative effect was that the total-addressable-market number embedded in investor presentations quietly narrowed. The structural asymmetry was punishing: an adverse ruling cost OppFi a state permanently (or until the law changed) while a favourable ruling merely confirmed ground it already held.

## Charge-Off Volatility and the Cycle Scar

The 2022–2023 vintages left a deep scar: elevated charge-offs, swings from profitability to net loss, and origination compression. The 2024 recovery proved the underwriting tightening worked, but demonstrated how quickly non-prime performance can deteriorate. A second credit dislocation would restart the cycle.

## Warehouse Risk and Rate Sensitivity

OppFi's funding model amplified both the credit-cycle and rate risks. The company funded its purchase of receivables from bank partners primarily through revolving warehouse credit facilities extended by major bank lenders. Those facilities carried floating-rate pricing, renewing periodically under negotiated terms. The combination of floating-rate cost of funds against a portfolio of fixed-rate consumer loans created structural margin compression whenever short-term rates rose, precisely the condition that prevailed through 2022 and 2023 as the Federal Reserve's tightening cycle pushed SOFR above five percent.

Facility renewal risk compounded the interest-rate exposure. Warehouse lenders reassess counterparty credit quality at renewal, and a platform lender reporting elevated charge-offs and net losses — as OppFi was during the 2022-2023 trough — presents a less attractive borrower than in calmer conditions. The concentration of funding across a limited number of bank facilities meant that a single lender's withdrawal or material tightening of advance-rate terms could force a reduction in origination capacity with little warning. The company disclosed these risks in standard 10-K fashion, but the qualitative language understated the operational reality: warehouse availability was a binding constraint on growth, and its terms moved inversely with OppFi's credit quality.

## Governance: The Up-C Overhang

The up-C structure (detailed in *Business Model*) created governance complexity: Todd Schwartz retained effective voting control through Class B shares, insulating management from market discipline. The TRA transferred economic value from public shareholders to insiders at each exchange event, reinforcing the structural subordination of public minority shareholders.

## Federal Regulatory Exposure and CFPB Dynamics

The federal regulatory landscape shifted meaningfully with the change of administration in January 2025. The CFPB under the Biden administration had been an active antagonist of high-rate bank-partnership lending, pursuing rulemaking on small-dollar credit and publishing interpretive guidance that questioned the scope of federal preemption for fintech-bank arrangements. The Trump administration's move to curtail CFPB enforcement activity in early 2025 reduced the near-term federal regulatory pressure on OppFi's model, but it did not eliminate it — the Bureau's enabling statute remained intact, appropriations litigation notwithstanding, and a future administration could reconstitute its enforcement posture. Congressional Democrats continued to advance versions of the Veterans and Consumers Fair Credit Act, which would impose a 36% APR cap federally across all consumer credit including bank-originated loans, effectively prohibiting OppFi's product nationally. The bill had not passed as of the frozen window, but its periodic reintroduction served as a standing reminder that the regulatory floor beneath the bank-partnership model was political as much as legal.

## Competitive Pressure

Enova and OneMain operate at larger scale with structural advantages (Enova's diversification; OneMain's direct-licensing model without true-lender exposure). BNPL platforms add margin pressure on customer acquisition cost. (See *Competitive Position* chapter for detailed analysis.)

Together, the six risk vectors — state-level litigation, credit-cycle volatility, warehouse funding fragility, governance structure, federal regulatory exposure, and competitive intensity — constituted a risk profile unusual even within the non-prime category.

chapters.title: Litigation resolution paths, multi-product expansion, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The fork in the road: litigation as the master variable

The strategic horizon for OppFi from 2026 through the end of the decade divides into two fundamentally different businesses depending on a single variable: how the accumulated weight of state-level true-lender litigation resolves. Each adverse ruling costs a state's origination volume and invites copycat enforcement elsewhere; each favourable resolution validates the bank-partnership architecture.

## Path A: compression and the adverse-outcome scenario

Under this scenario, OppFi's addressable market shrinks toward states with no effective usury ceiling. Management's mitigants: deepening penetration in favourable jurisdictions, accelerating fee-based revenue, and pivoting toward white-label servicing income. The OppFi Card, operating under more settled credit-card preemption, would carry survivability the core OppLoans product could not claim.

## Path B: validated model and the expansion scenario

If major state cases settle on terms preserving rate exportation, OppFi's addressable market expands. The Valid When Made doctrine, reinforced by 2020–2021 OCC/FDIC rulemakings, provides the federal legal anchor. In this scenario, the litigation years would be recast as forced operational discipline that eliminated undercapitalised competitors.

## The OppFi Card as hedge and product wedge

The OppFi Card serves dual purposes: a hedge against adverse true-lender rulings (it operates under more settled credit-card preemption) and a customer-retention mechanism for borrowers who graduate from installment lending. Per-account economics run lower but customer tenure extends, producing more predictable cash flow.

## Consumer-credit cycle: the 2026 positioning

By 2026, the credit cycle that devastated 2022–2023 vintages was substantially digested. The 2024–2025 books carried lower loss rates, warehouse facilities were renegotiated at tighter spreads, and net revenue per originated dollar improved. The forward question: whether 2026–2027 growth can be pursued without re-opening the charge-off cycle.

## The 2026-2030 strategic posture

In both litigation scenarios, OppFi invests in technology platform capability, product breadth, and proprietary data assets that competitors without equivalent origination volume cannot replicate. The up-C dual-class structure insulates strategic decision-making from short-cycle shareholder pressure. OppFi's differentiation resides less in the loan product itself and more in its thesis that the non-prime consumer deserves a technology-mediated path toward mainstream credit access. Whether that thesis survives the litigation crucible intact — or is forced into structural adaptation toward a smaller market — the decade ahead will determine.
